2026-09-14-bias-variance-tradeoff.png.caption:
The bias-variance tradeoff, explained in one curve 📉

Every model faces this: go too simple and you're consistently wrong (bias). Go too complex and you memorize noise instead of signal (variance). The best model isn't the most powerful one — it's the one that balances both.

🔍 How to find your sweet spot: cross-validation, learning curves, or a held-out validation set.

Correlation isn't causation 🔎

Two variables can move together without either one causing the other. A hidden third factor — a confounder — can be driving both at once. Before you claim causation, rule out confounders, reverse causation, and plain coincidence.

2026-09-17-precision-vs-recall.png.caption:
Precision vs. recall: two different questions 🎯

Precision asks: of everything I flagged, how much was actually right? Recall asks: of everything that truly mattered, how much did I catch? A model can be great at one and terrible at the other — choose based on the real cost of a false positive vs. a missed case.

2026-09-18-central-limit-theorem.png.caption:
The Central Limit Theorem, visually 🔔

Take repeated random samples and average each one — no matter how skewed the original population is, the distribution of those sample means converges toward a normal curve as sample size grows. It's why confidence intervals and t-tests work almost everywhere.

2026-09-19-train-test-leakage.png.caption:
Data leakage: your model is cheating 🚨

If information from the test set sneaks into training — even indirectly, through a scaler or feature fit on the full dataset — your model looks great on paper and quietly fails the moment it meets real data. Avoid it by splitting first, then fitting every transform on the training set only.

2026-09-20-ab-testing.png.caption:
Is that A/B test result even real? 🧪

Variant B looks better — but with small samples, random noise alone can produce a gap this size. A significance test asks: how likely is this result if there were truly no difference at all? Before you ship the winner, check sample size, test duration, and whether p < 0.05.

2026-09-21-l1-vs-l2-regularization.png.caption:
L1 vs. L2: two ways to penalize ⚖️

Both add a penalty for large weights, but the shape of that penalty matters. L1's sharp corners tend to zero out weights entirely (built-in feature selection). L2's smooth circle shrinks everything a little. Rule of thumb: L1 for sparse, interpretable models; L2 when most features carry at least some signal.

2026-09-22-confidence-intervals.png.caption:
What a 95% confidence interval really means 📐

It's NOT "a 95% chance the true value is in this one interval." It means: if you repeated this study many times, about 95% of the intervals you'd build would contain the true value — this one might not.

2026-09-23-k-fold-cross-validation.png.caption:
One test set isn't enough — use k folds 🔁

Split the data into k parts. Train on k-1 of them, validate on the one left out, then rotate which part is held out until every fold has had a turn. Average the k scores for a far more reliable performance estimate. Common choice: k = 5 or k = 10.
